name: Progressive overload hypertrophy training

lead: Progressive overload means gradually increasing the demand placed on muscles over time, by adding weight, repetitions, sets or other stress, so they keep adapting and growing. It is a standard principle in strength and hypertrophy training and is discussed in lifting communities as the basis of getting bigger.
Research summarised by encyclopedias links hypertrophy to mechanical tension, total training volume and progressive overload, while the best way to apply the principle is still studied.

paras: Resistance training under greater-than-normal demand triggers adaptation: neural changes first, then increases in muscle mass and connective-tissue strength [1]. Mechanical tension is the currently accepted theory of hypertrophy, activating mTOR signaling and muscle protein synthesis, though exact mechanisms are not fully understood [2].

Wikipedia notes that excessive training can cause overtraining and that periodization is used to help prevent it [1]. Injury risk depends on technique, load and individual factors, which the cited encyclopedia entries do not quantify.

lead: Progressive overload is a training principle in which the stress placed on the musculoskeletal and nervous systems is gradually increased so that strength and muscle mass continue to develop [1].

In looksmaxxing and lifting communities it is treated as the core of muscle-building for physique, and it underlies discussions of routines, splits and periodization. The concept is long established in exercise science and is cited in guidelines such as those of the American College of Sports Medicine [2].
Evidence broadly supports the principle that training volume and progressive overload relate to hypertrophy; how much to progress, and by which variable, is still examined in research [3][2].
infobox: Legend of Milo of Croton (6th century BC); formalised by Thomas DeLorme in the 1940s [1]

paras: Wikipedia cites the legend of Milo of Croton, a late 6th-century BC Greek athlete said to have lifted a calf daily as it grew into a bull, as the earliest mention of the idea [1]. It credits physician Thomas DeLorme with developing the method in the 1940s while rehabilitating soldiers after World War II, including a 1944 case at Gardiner General Hospital in Chicago [1].

Wikipedia states that adaptation slows or stops unless stress increases, with neuromuscular adaptations arriving first and muscle mass, connective-tissue strength and cross-section later [1]. In the hypertrophy literature, mechanical tension is described as the current accepted theory, and microtrauma correlates poorly with the amount of growth [3].

Training volume, defined as sets times repetitions times load, is described as one of the most important variables, with research reporting a positive relationship between volume and hypertrophy [2][4]. Long-term hypertrophy appears to depend more on total volume and progressive overload than on repetition tempo [3]. For frequency, more weekly sessions generally produce larger strength gains, but with equalized volume frequency had no influence on strength; for muscle growth, two sessions per week produced greater effects than one, and whether three beats two is undetermined [2][4].

Programs that vary load across time, such as linear, block and undulating periodization, are used to manage fatigue and overtraining; undulating models produced better one-repetition-maximum gains than non-periodized training, while for hypertrophy daily undulating performed similarly to traditional models [4].

Many human resistance-training trials and meta-analyses exist on volume, frequency and periodization; the findings summarised in encyclopedia entries are cited above [3][2][4]. No trial in this material tests the term "progressive overload" as a standalone intervention against none.
